title: The Frog and the Lizard
summary: A thoughtful lizard keeps warning its proud frog friend about small dangers, but the frog angrily refuses every warning. In the end the lizard learns when it is wiser to step back.
from: Animal fable, Chhattisgarh (from Twente, Folk Tales of Chhattisgarh India)
levelReason: The supplied text uses clear, everyday words with a few harder ones (retorted, flatterers, interfering, offended). Sentences average about 10 words and are joined with simple connectors such as "But" and "After some time". The ending states the lesson in plain words. That fits Level 2 better than the very short sentences of Level 1 or the richer style of Level 3.

en: Long ago, a frog and a lizard lived near a river in Chhattisgarh. They were very good friends. They spent their days together.
The lizard was thoughtful and careful. The frog was proud. He did not like being told what to do.
One morning, the frog jumped into the river. He swam along with the water. The lizard watched from the bank. It felt worried.
“My friend!” it called. “Be careful! You may drown!”
The frog was annoyed. “Let your mother and sister drown!” he shouted. “Why should I drown? Can’t you see I am swimming across just fine?”
The lizard said nothing. Soon the frog climbed out. He sat on a big pile of thorns.
The lizard saw him there. “Oh, my friend! Be careful! The thorns may prick you!” it said.
The frog was upset again. “Let your parents be pricked!” he said. “Can’t you see I am moving the thorns away?”
The lizard did not argue. After a while, the frog sat down on a heap of dung. He looked happy there.
The lizard looked at him with worry. “My poor friend! You are getting so dirty!” it said.
The frog was angry a third time. “Your parents are dirty!” he said. “Can’t you see I am making cakes for people who flatter me?”

Now the lizard understood. Its friend did not want any advice. There was no use in warning him more. From that day, the lizard stopped getting into the frog’s business. The frog did what he liked. The lizard quietly did its own work.
So the lizard learned something. Some people get angry even when you try to help them.
Moral: Advice helps only when a person wants to listen. If someone keeps refusing kind help, it is sometimes wiser to step back.
hi: बहुत पहले की बात है। छत्तीसगढ़ में एक नदी के पास एक मेंढक और एक छिपकली रहते थे। वे बहुत अच्छे दोस्त थे। वे अपने दिन साथ बिताते थे।
छिपकली समझदार और सावधान थी। मेंढक घमंडी था। उसे कोई कुछ करने को कहे, यह उसे पसंद नहीं था।
एक सुबह मेंढक नदी में कूद गया। वह पानी के साथ तैरने लगा। छिपकली किनारे से देख रही थी। उसे चिंता हुई।
“मेरे दोस्त!” उसने पुकारा। “सँभलकर! तुम डूब सकते हो!”
मेंढक चिढ़ गया। “तेरी माँ और बहन डूबें!” वह चिल्लाया। “मैं क्यों डूबूँगा? क्या तुझे दिखता नहीं कि मैं आराम से नदी पार कर रहा हूँ?”
छिपकली चुप रही। थोड़ी देर में मेंढक बाहर निकल आया। वह काँटों के एक बड़े ढेर पर बैठ गया।
छिपकली ने उसे वहाँ देखा। “अरे मेरे दोस्त! सँभलकर! काँटे चुभ सकते हैं!” उसने कहा।
मेंढक फिर नाराज़ हो गया। “तेरे माँ-बाप को चुभें!” उसने कहा। “क्या तुझे दिखता नहीं कि मैं काँटे हटा रहा हूँ?”
छिपकली ने बहस नहीं की। कुछ देर बाद मेंढक गोबर के एक ढेर पर जा बैठा। वह वहाँ खुश दिख रहा था।
छिपकली ने चिंता से उसे देखा। “मेरे बेचारे दोस्त! तुम तो बहुत गंदे हो रहे हो!” उसने कहा।
मेंढक तीसरी बार गुस्सा हो गया। “तेरे माँ-बाप गंदे हैं!” उसने कहा। “क्या तुझे दिखता नहीं कि मैं चापलूसों के लिए पकवान बना रहा हूँ?”

अब छिपकली समझ गई। उसका दोस्त कोई सलाह सुनना ही नहीं चाहता था। उसे और टोकने का कोई फ़ायदा नहीं था। उस दिन से छिपकली ने मेंढक के मामलों में दखल देना छोड़ दिया। मेंढक अपनी मर्ज़ी से चलता रहा। छिपकली चुपचाप अपना काम करती रही।
इस तरह छिपकली ने एक बात सीखी। कुछ लोग मदद करने पर भी गुस्सा हो जाते हैं।
सीख: सलाह तभी काम आती है जब कोई सुनना चाहे। जब कोई बार-बार भली बात ठुकराए, तो कभी-कभी पीछे हट जाना ही समझदारी है।

en: Once upon a time, a frog and a lizard lived near a river in the countryside of Chhattisgarh. They were very good friends and often spent their days together.
The lizard was thoughtful and cautious, while the frog was rather proud and disliked being told what to do.
One morning, the frog jumped into a river and began swimming along with the current. The lizard, watching from the riverbank, became worried.
“My friend!” it called out. “Be careful! I am afraid you might drown!”
The frog became annoyed. “Let your mother and sister drown!” he shouted. “Why should I drown? Can’t you see that I am crossing the river perfectly well?”
The lizard fell silent. A little later, the frog climbed out of the water and sat on a large pile of thorns.
The lizard noticed where its friend had settled. “Oh, my friend! Be careful. Those thorns might prick you!” it warned.
But the frog was offended once again. “Let your parents be pricked!” he replied. “Can’t you see that I am simply removing the thorns?”
The lizard decided not to argue. After some time, the frog moved to a nearby heap of dung and settled down comfortably.
The lizard looked at him with concern. “My poor friend! You are getting yourself terribly dirty!” it exclaimed.
The frog became angry for the third time. “Your parents are dirty!” he retorted. “Can’t you see that I am preparing cakes for flatterers?”

The lizard finally understood that its friend had no intention of listening to any advice. It decided that there was no point in warning him any further. From that day onwards, the lizard stopped interfering in the frog’s affairs. The frog continued doing whatever he pleased, while the lizard quietly went about its own business.
And so, the lizard learned that some people become angry even when others are trying to help them.
Moral: Advice is useful only when someone is willing to listen. When a person repeatedly rejects good intentions, sometimes it is wiser to step back.

questions.q: Why did the lizard keep warning the frog? What did it want for its friend?
Why did the frog get angry each time the lizard spoke? What does that tell you about him?
The frog goes into the river, onto the thorns, and onto the dung. How does each answer he gives show that he will not admit a mistake?
After the third time, the lizard stopped warning the frog. Was this a good decision? Explain.
What do you think "cakes for flatterers" means in the frog's answer? What was he really doing?

en: Once upon a time, a frog and a lizard lived beside a river in the Chhattisgarh countryside. They were the best of friends and passed most of their days together.
The lizard was thoughtful and cautious by nature, while the frog was proud and bristled whenever anyone tried to tell him what to do.
One morning, the frog leapt into the river and let the current carry him along. From the bank, the lizard watched anxiously.
“My friend!” it called out. “Do be careful! I am afraid you might drown!”
The frog flared up in annoyance. “Let your mother and sister drown!” he shouted. “Why should I drown? Can’t you see I am crossing this river perfectly well?”
The lizard fell silent. Some time later, the frog climbed out of the water and settled himself on a great pile of thorns.
The lizard noticed where its friend had sat down. “Oh, my friend, take care! Those thorns might prick you!” it warned.
Once again, the frog took offence. “Let your parents be pricked!” he snapped. “Can’t you see I am simply clearing away the thorns?”
The lizard chose not to argue. After a while, the frog moved to a nearby heap of dung and sat down there, quite at ease.
The lizard watched him with deep concern. “My poor friend!” it cried. “You are getting yourself terribly dirty!”
For the third time, the frog’s temper boiled over. “Your parents are dirty!” he retorted. “Can’t you see I am preparing cakes for flatterers?”

At last the lizard understood that its friend had no intention of heeding any advice, and that further warnings would be pointless. From that day on, it stopped meddling in the frog’s affairs. The frog went on doing exactly as he pleased, while the lizard quietly minded its own business.
And so the lizard learned a hard truth: some people grow angry even when others are only trying to help them.
Moral: Advice is useful only when someone is willing to listen. When a person repeatedly rejects good intentions, it can be wiser to step back.

मेंढक ने एक बार फिर बुरा मान लिया। “तेरे माँ-बाप को चुभें!” उसने तुनककर कहा। “क्या तुझे दिखता नहीं कि मैं तो बस काँटे साफ़ कर रहा हूँ?”
छिपकली ने बहस न करना ही ठीक समझा। कुछ देर बाद मेंढक पास के गोबर के ढेर पर जा पहुँचा और वहाँ बड़े आराम से बैठ गया।

सीख: सलाह तभी काम की होती है जब कोई उसे सुनने को तैयार हो। जब कोई बार-बार भली नीयत को ठुकराता है, तो पीछे हट जाना ज़्यादा समझदारी हो सकती है।

questions.q: When should we keep giving a friend advice, and when is it right to step back? Was the lizard right to stop?
How might the frog describe what happened? Why might he have felt that the lizard was treating him like a child?
The moral says advice is useful only when someone is willing to listen. Why do you think some people find it hard to accept help or a warning?
The frog turns each mistake into a boast, as if he meant to do it. What does this tell you about pride and the fear of being seen as wrong?
In school, online or at home, how can we give advice in a way that someone is more likely to hear? How can we become better listeners ourselves?

scenes.p: A quiet riverbank in the Chhattisgarh countryside with reeds, a few mango trees and a sandy shore in warm morning light. A small green frog with a puffed-up chest and a slender brown-grey house lizard with a long curved tail sit side by side on a flat rock, friendly together. Soft storybook illustration, same character looks in every scene.

scenes.t: The frog swims, the lizard worries
scenes.th: मेंढक तैरता है, छिपकली चिंता करती है
scenes.p: The green frog swims confidently in the river current, chin raised and proud, while the slender brown-grey lizard on the bank leans forward with an anxious face and one hand raised, calling a warning. The frog looks back annoyed. Sunlit water, ripples. Mood: worry against stubbornness.

The green frog sits on a large pile of thorny branches on the bank, proudly lifting a few thorns aside with a hand while looking cross, as if he is clearing them. The brown-grey lizard stands a few steps away, concerned, finger raised in warning. Midday light, dry scrub behind. Mood: stubborn pride.

scenes.t: The frog and the dung heap
scenes.p: The green frog sits on a heap of cow dung at the edge of a village path, looking smug, shaping little round lumps like cakes, his skin streaked with brown, drawn in a funny, gentle, non-gross cartoon way. The lizard looks at him with deep concern from a stone wall. Late afternoon light. Mood: gentle comedy and worry.

The brown-grey lizard turns away and walks along the bank with a calm, thoughtful face, while the green frog behind it carries on, busy with his own doings, not noticing. Evening glow on the river, long shadows. Mood: quiet, bittersweet.

The brown-grey lizard rests alone on a warm rock beside the river at sunset, gazing at the water with a wise, peaceful look; far away in the background, the small green frog is splashing at the water's edge. Mood: calm, reflective, with a touch of sadness.

artStyle.note: Bastar wall painting, made by communities such as the Gond, Halba and Bhatra, traditionally uses a limited palette of white lime, red ochre, charcoal black and yellow clay, with strongly outlined, flat figures and geometric borders, and animals are a common subject. We could not confirm that this fable belongs to those communities, so use this only as gentle inspiration for colour and line: warm earth tones, bold outlines, simple geometric borders. Do not label the images as Bastar art.

imagine: Imagine you are sitting on the riverbank beside the lizard when the frog climbs onto the thorns. What do you whisper to the lizard? What sounds do you hear around the river?
create: Draw the frog on the heap and write one speech bubble for each of them. Or write a short ending where the frog finally asks the lizard for help, and decide how the lizard replies.

about.where: Chhattisgarh is a state in central India, with villages, forests and rivers. This story is listed as a folktale of Chhattisgarh, in a book of tales published in 1938.
about.community: The sources we have do not say which community first told this version, so we are not guessing. This is one version from one source, and other tellers may tell it differently.
about.tradition: Animal fables, in which small creatures behave like people, are told to children in many parts of India and the world. They often end with a short saying that tells listeners what to think about.
about.shared: Stories about a friend who will not take advice are told in many cultures. Here the frog's answers are funny but also sharp, and the lizard's choice at the end is the heart of the story.
about.matters: The story helps us think about listening, pride and kindness. It reminds us that good advice is given with care and also that we are free to choose when to step back.
